## Overview

`estimateH2()` estimates SNP heritability from GWAS summary statistics and
an LD reference, under the model settings an `H2EstimateParam` gives
(`param`). Each published estimator is a setting of one model, differing in
what it fits and what it needs (`?H2EstimateParam` lists every setting):

| Method | Statistic / criterion | LD input |
|---|---|---|
| S-LDSC (Finucane 2015) | variants / regression on LD scores | `LdScore` |
| g-LDSC (Xiong 2024) | variants / GLS on full block LD | `LdScore` + matrices |
| LDER (Song 2022) | eigen / regression | `LdEigen` |
| HDL (Ning 2020), the default | eigen / likelihood | `LdEigen` |

`estimateStratifiedH2()` fits any of them stratified by annotations, adding a
per-annotation enrichment table. These estimators are genome-wide: each gives
one estimate per study. Each gene's heritability in its cis window,
from QTL summary statistics or individual-level QTL data, is
`estimateLocalH2()`'s. Either way the result is an `H2Estimate`, a
collection with one row per estimate: its identity (`study`, `context`,
`trait`) and values (`h2`, `h2_se`, ...) are columns, a cis estimate's
element is the window it covers, and `h2EstimateParam()` returns the
settings of the model every estimate in it was fitted under.

There is a second, separate track in the package: when stratified LDSC has
already been run externally by [polyfun][pf], `sldscPostprocessingPipeline()`
postprocesses those outputs. Both tracks are covered below.

[pf]: https://github.com/omerwe/polyfun

```{r load-packages}
library(pecotmr)
data(ldScoreExample, ldEigenExample)
ldScoreExample
```

Both bundled references describe the same `r length(ldScoreExample)`
variants across `r length(ldBlocks(ldScoreExample))` chr22 LD blocks, so the
four methods can be compared on one dataset. Their LD is that of a reference
panel of `r ldPanelNSamples(ldScoreExample)` people simulated from the chr22
LD of the de-identified `protocol_example` panel. That panel itself is a
sketch of 60 people: far too few for these estimators, which correct for the
noise in a reference's LD, so the examples carry the LD of a large panel
drawn from it instead (`inst/scripts/build_h2_examples.R`).

## Variants must line up

Every estimator reads the z-scores positionally, indexed by the LD
reference's own variant order — nothing is matched on variant ID along the
way. `estimateH2()` and `estimateStratifiedH2()` therefore check up front
that the summary statistics, the annotations and the reference describe the
same variants, in the same order, on the same genome build, and refuse to run
otherwise.

The practical consequence: build the summary statistics *from* the reference
rather than alongside it.

```{r simulate-gwas}
# A GWAS simulated on this reference so the true h2 is known: z is drawn
# from the standard model z ~ N(0, N R diag(v) R + R), block by block.
M <- length(ldScoreExample)
nGwas <- 10000
h2True <- 0.4
perSnpVar <- rep(h2True / M, M)

set.seed(1)
z <- numeric(M)
for (block in ldMatrixList(ldScoreExample)) {
    idx <- block$snpIdx
    p <- length(idx)
    sigma <- nGwas * (block$R %*% diag(perSnpVar[idx], p) %*% block$R) +
        block$R
    e <- eigen((sigma + t(sigma)) / 2, symmetric = TRUE)
    z[idx] <- as.vector(e$vectors %*% (sqrt(pmax(e$values, 0)) * rnorm(p)))
}

gr <- as(ldScoreExample, "GRanges")
S4Vectors::mcols(gr) <- S4Vectors::DataFrame(
    SNP = names(ldScoreExample),
    A1 = S4Vectors::mcols(ldScoreExample)$A1,
    A2 = S4Vectors::mcols(ldScoreExample)$A2,
    Z = z,
    N = as.integer(nGwas)
)
```

```{r gwas-sumstats, eval = hasPlinkMatrix}
gwas <- GwasSumStats(
    studyName = "trait1",
    entry = list(gr),
    genome = unique(unname(GenomeInfoDb::genome(ldScoreExample))),
    ldReference = readGenotypes(
        system.file("extdata", "toy_ref.bed", package = "pecotmr")
    )
)
```

## Estimating heritability

```{r estimate, eval = hasPlinkMatrix}
# Each method's settings, as ?H2EstimateParam lists them; HDL's are the
# default (NULL).
settings <- list(
    sldsc = H2EstimateParam(
        statistic = "variant",
        criterion = "regression",
        noise = "free",
        crossNoise = "window",
        referenceNoise = "unbiasedR2",
        sampleSize = "median",
        inference = "jackknife",
        procedures = H2RegressionParam(
            initialWeights = "moments",
            ldRedundancy = TRUE,
            iterations = 2,
            twoStage = TRUE,
            chi2Threshold = 30
        )
    ),
    gldsc = H2EstimateParam(
        statistic = "variant",
        criterion = "gls",
        noise = "free",
        crossNoise = "window",
        referenceNoise = "none",
        sampleSize = "median",
        inference = "jackknife"
    ),
    lder = NULL,
    hdl = H2EstimateParam(
        criterion = "likelihood",
        noise = "free",
        crossNoise = "window",
        referenceNoise = "eigenTerm",
        truncation = H2TruncationParam(
            fraction = 1,
            of = "variants",
            maxPerSample = NULL,
            minimum = 1
        ),
        sampleSize = "median",
        inference = "jackknife",
        procedures = H2LikelihoodParam(
            interceptBounds = c(0, 10),
            varianceFloor = exp(-10),
            regressionStart = TRUE,
            h2Starts = 0.1,
            interceptStarts = 1,
            mustBeatNull = FALSE,
            halfBoundaryP = FALSE,
            maxit = 1000
        )
    )
)
methods <- names(settings)
refs <- list(
    sldsc = ldScoreExample,
    gldsc = ldScoreExample,
    lder = ldEigenExample,
    hdl = ldEigenExample
)
estimates <- lapply(methods, function(m) {
    suppressWarnings(estimateH2(gwas, refs[[m]], param = settings[[m]]))
})
names(estimates) <- methods

data.frame(
    method = methods,
    h2 = round(vapply(estimates, heritabilityEstimate, numeric(1)), 3),
    se = round(vapply(estimates, heritabilityEstimateSe, numeric(1)), 3),
    row.names = NULL
)
```

The true value is `r h2True`. Three of the four land close to it; S-LDSC
comes in low, and that is worth understanding rather than tuning away.

**S-LDSC is attenuated because the reference is small.** LD score
regression is a genome-scale method — real analyses regress over roughly a
million variants. On 1300 the intercept is not identifiable: an unweighted
OLS on this same data returns an intercept several times its true value of
1, and the heritability absorbs the difference. LDER is the least
sensitive to reference size, which is why its settings are the default.

All four are checked against their reference implementations — [ldsc][ldsc],
[HDL][hdl], [LDER][lder] and [gldsc][gldsc] — on identical inputs: HDL agrees
exactly, LDER to machine precision, gLDSC to ~3e-8 and S-LDSC to ~1e-6. The
small residuals are a ridge on the weighted solve, which keeps an exactly
singular design from returning `NA`. Agreement holds even where the
reference implementations misbehave, such as an S-LDSC intercept below 1 or
a negative partitioned heritability.

One deliberate difference: LDER here clamps negative eigenvalues before
forming its regression weights. A real, rank-deficient LD block decomposes
with a tail of tiny negative values that are floating-point noise, and the
original LDER implementation takes `sqrt()` of the resulting negative weight
and aborts. The clamp changes nothing wherever the original runs.

[ldsc]: https://github.com/bulik/ldsc
[hdl]: https://github.com/zhenin/HDL
[lder]: https://github.com/shuangsong0110/LDER
[gldsc]: https://github.com/xzw20046/gldsc

**HDL has a reference-size limit, and it tells you when it hits it.** It
is the only one of the four that models reference-panel *noise* explicitly:
its likelihood subtracts a term scaling as `1/nRef` from the modelled
variance. Once the reference is small relative to the GWAS, that term
outgrows the signal, the modelled variance is driven to its floor across
most eigen-directions, and the optimiser walks the intercept out to the top
of its range — returning a number that reflects that bound rather than the
data. This reference's `r ldPanelNSamples(ldEigenExample)` people are plenty:
even at `N = 1e5` HDL recovers about 0.40 for a true 0.4. Against a
1,000-person panel at that `N` it drifts to about 0.57 and warns that the fit
sits on a bound. If HDL disagrees sharply with the others, check for that
warning and compare `sampleSize()` against `ldPanelNSamples()`.

A standard error of zero, or an estimate pinned at a boundary, almost always
means the reference is too small rather than that the trait has no
heritability. The block jackknife needs at least two LD blocks and wants many
more; `estimateH2()` refuses a single-block reference outright.

Every fit above weighs each variant alike, the per-SD model. The frequency
exponent `alpha` of `H2EstimateParam()` weighs each variant's effect variance
by its heterozygosity in the reference, [2p(1 - p)]^(1 + alpha): 0 is the
per-allele model and LDAK's -0.25 lies between. The reference supplies the
frequencies: the `MAF` an `LdEigen` or `LdScore` records when built from
`LdMatrix` blocks with an `AF` column, or else its genotype panel's. S-LDSC's
weighted LD scores are formed from each block's LD, so a scores-only
`LdScore` serves it only at the default.

**A case/control study's heritability is on the observed scale.** Give its
`GwasSumStats` the study's case and control counts (`nCase`, `nControl`)
and the trait's population `prevalence`. The estimate's `h2_liability`
columns then hold it on the liability scale too (Lee et al. 2011). The
share of cases that conversion reads is one half where `summaryStatsQc()`
has set N to the effective sample size, as it does by default for a study
with counts. A quantitative trait records no counts and has no liability
scale. Its `varY` does not enter the fit either, which reads z alone. A
pair from `estimateLocalRg()` with such a GWAS side has that side's
heritability and the genetic covariance on the liability scale too
(`h2_2_liability`, `covariance_liability`); rg is the same on either scale.

## Building an LD reference

The bundled references were built with `buildLdEigen()` / `buildLdScore()`,
which turn an LD reference into the statistic each estimator needs. The
reference comes **per LD block**: a genotype panel together with the blocks
to cut it into, or one `LdMatrix` per block. One block has no jackknife.

```{r build-ref, eval=FALSE}
panel <- readGenotypes(plink2Prefix = "/path/to/reference.chr22")
blocks <- "/path/to/ld_blocks.bed" # a BED file, or a GRanges

ldEigen <- buildLdEigen(panel, ldBlocks = blocks, genome = "hg38")
ldScore <- buildLdScore(panel, ldBlocks = blocks, genome = "hg38")

# Or from LD matrices you built, one LdMatrix per block:
ldScore <- buildLdScore(list(ldBlock1, ldBlock2, ldBlock3), genome = "hg38")
```

`nSamples` (the reference panel size) and the genome build default to what
the reference records: a panel's sample count (for a stochastic sketch, the
effective size of its LD), or the `nSamples` of each `LdMatrix`. The panel
size matters beyond HDL: LD scores sum ldsc's unbiased r²,
`r^2 - (1 - r^2) / (n - 2)`, so `n` should be the number of samples the LD
was estimated from.
`buildLdScore(keepLdMatrices = FALSE)` drops the per-block matrices, which
shrinks the object by roughly an order of magnitude — but only unstratified
`"sldsc"` can use the result, since `"gldsc"` and stratified `"sldsc"` both
form their per-annotation scores from each block's LD. An `LdScore` or
`LdEigen` built from a genotype panel stores none of it: it keeps the panel
and reads each block's LD when an estimator reaches that block, so every
method runs on it while only one block's LD is in memory at a time.

## Stratified estimation and enrichment

`estimateStratifiedH2()` partitions heritability across the annotations of
an `AnnotationMatrix`. The model settings an `H2EstimateParam` gives choose
the fit: the variants by regression (S-LDSC's) or by GLS (g-LDSC's), the
eigen statistic by regression (LDER's) or by likelihood (HDL's, sHDL
stratified, the default, slower than LDER's regression with many
annotations); `?H2EstimateParam` lists the settings that reproduce each.
The annotation rows must line up with the reference, exactly as the summary
statistics do.

```{r annotate, eval = hasPlinkMatrix}
# An illustrative annotation over the first half of the reference, simulated
# to carry three times the per-variant heritability of the rest.
inA <- seq_len(M) <= M / 2
perSnpVarStrat <- ifelse(inA, 0.225 / sum(inA), 0.075 / sum(!inA))

set.seed(1)
zStrat <- numeric(M)
for (block in ldMatrixList(ldScoreExample)) {
    idx <- block$snpIdx
    p <- length(idx)
    sigma <- nGwas *
        (block$R %*% diag(perSnpVarStrat[idx], p) %*% block$R) +
        block$R
    e <- eigen((sigma + t(sigma)) / 2, symmetric = TRUE)
    zStrat[idx] <- as.vector(
        e$vectors %*% (sqrt(pmax(e$values, 0)) * rnorm(p))
    )
}
S4Vectors::mcols(gr)$Z <- zStrat
gwasStrat <- GwasSumStats(
    studyName = "trait1",
    entry = list(gr),
    genome = unique(unname(GenomeInfoDb::genome(ldScoreExample))),
    ldReference = readGenotypes(
        system.file("extdata", "toy_ref.bed", package = "pecotmr")
    )
)

annot <- AnnotationMatrix(
    matrix(as.integer(inA), ncol = 1, dimnames = list(NULL, "annotA")),
    as(ldScoreExample, "GRanges"),
    data.frame(name = "annotA", tier = "baseline", type = "binary"),
    genome = unique(unname(GenomeInfoDb::genome(ldScoreExample)))
)
```

```{r enrichment, eval = hasPlinkMatrix}
# g-LDSC's settings: the variants by GLS, a free intercept, the median
# sample size and the jackknife over the reference's LD blocks.
gldsc <- H2EstimateParam(
    statistic = "variant",
    criterion = "gls",
    noise = "free",
    crossNoise = "window",
    referenceNoise = "none",
    sampleSize = "median",
    inference = "jackknife"
)
strat <- estimateStratifiedH2(gwasStrat, ldScoreExample, annot, param = gldsc)
as.data.frame(stratifiedHeritabilityEnrichment(strat))[, c(
    "annotation",
    "tau",
    "enrichment",
    "enrichmentSe",
    "propH2",
    "propSnps"
)]
```

`enrichment` is the proportion of heritability divided by the proportion of
variants: above 1 means the annotation carries more heritability than its
share of the genome. The simulated truth here is 1.5 — three times the
per-variant heritability on half the variants puts 75% of it in `annotA` —
and the estimate is directionally right but attenuated, again a consequence
of the reference's size rather than of the annotation.

`enrichmentP` is ldsc's t test of the per-variant heritability inside the
annotation against outside it, for every estimator. Those shares are only
shares for values in [0, 1], the domain enrichment is defined on (Dey et al.
2020), so for an annotation with values outside it the enrichment columns are
`NA` and `tau` is the summary to read; `standardizeTauStar()` puts it on a
scale comparable across annotations. Inside [0, 1], the enrichment of a
continuous annotation still depends on its zero meaning "not in the
annotation": `(x + 3) / 100` and `(x - min(x)) / max(x - min(x))` fit the same
model but report different enrichments.

Annotations come from files via `readAnnotations()`, which reads BED, BigWig
and LDSC `.annot` formats at a given set of variant positions:

```{r read-annotations, eval=FALSE}
annot <- readAnnotations(
    c(enhancer = "enhancers.bed", conservation = "phastCons.bw"),
    snpRanges = as(ldScoreExample, "GRanges"),
    genome = "hg38"
)
```

The `tier` column decides how each annotation is used: `"baseline"`
annotations enter the model and get an enrichment estimate, while
`"candidate"` annotations are scored against the fitted baseline, one score
test each, via `scoreStats()`. Every estimator calibrates that test by the
spread of its LD blocks' scores, as it does its standard errors, so it stays
valid when the regression weights are only approximately right. Molecular QTL
annotations built by `fineMappingAnnotations()` from fine-mapping results are
candidates by default. Every effect a fit keeps spreads a whole unit of
posterior over its variants, however weak its evidence, so its `maxCpp` and
`sumPip` columns carry some low-confidence mass; `types = c("maxCppCs",
"sumPipCs")` builds them from the effects that produced a credible set alone.

All four estimators fit the same baseline design. An all-ones base
annotation is added ahead of the baseline annotations unless they already
cover every variant between them, as a partition of the genome does. Without
it the variants no annotation covers would be modelled as carrying no
heritability. Beside the base, an annotation's coefficient is its excess over
the genome-wide rate, which is negative for a depleted annotation. Annotations
may overlap; each one's heritability is taken from the overlap-aware
partition \(A'A\tau\), and only the annotations you supplied are reported.

## Postprocessing external polyfun runs

The second track handles stratified LDSC that was run outside R by polyfun.
The readers load its outputs, `SldscData` bundles them, and the pipeline
does the computation — no file I/O of its own.

```{r sldsc-read}
sldscDir <- system.file("extdata", "sldsc", package = "pecotmr")
traitDir <- system.file("extdata", "sldsc_trait", package = "pecotmr")

annotTable <- readSldscAnnot(sldscDir)
frq <- readSldscFrq(sldscDir, plinkName = "reference.")

traitNames <- c(traitA = "sumstats", traitB = "sumstats2", traitC = "sumstats3")
runs <- lapply(traitNames, function(t) {
    readSldscTrait(file.path(traitDir, paste0(t, ".parquet")))
})
runs$traitA$categories
```

Those categories are a real baseline model — `Coding_UCSC`,
`Conserved_LindbladToh` and `Repressed_Hoffman`, each split into common and
low-frequency, plus `base` — with `ANNOT_0` as the target annotation under
test.

```{r sldsc-pipeline}
sldscData <- SldscData(
    annotData = annotTable,
    frqData = frq,
    traits = lapply(runs, function(r) list(single = list(r)))
)
result <- sldscPostprocessingPipeline(
    sldscData,
    targetCategories = "ANNOT_0"
)
as.data.frame(result$meta$enrichment)
```

The pipeline standardizes each trait's tau to Gazal tau\*, back-solves a
jackknife standard error for the enrichment statistic, and pools traits by
DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis. `sldscSubsetMeta()` re-runs
the meta over a subset of traits without refitting anything:

```{r sldsc-subset}
subset <- sldscSubsetMeta(result, subsetTraits = c("traitB", "traitC"))
unlist(subset$enrichment$ANNOT_0)
```

Each polyfun run may be a `single` target run or a `joint` one; supplying
both lets the pipeline report the target's enrichment from the single fit
alongside its coefficient from the joint fit.

### The postprocessing steps

`sldscPostprocessingPipeline()` is a wrapper over steps that are exported
individually, which is what you want when auditing a surprising number:

```{r sldsc-steps}
computeSldscMRef(sldscData, mafCutoff = 0.05) # the M_ref that scales tau*
isBinarySldscAnnot(sldscData) # binary vs continuous
```

`computeSldscAnnotSd()` gives the per-annotation standard deviation that
turns tau into Gazal tau\*, `standardizeSldscTrait()` does that
standardisation for one trait's run, and `metaSldscRandom()` is the
DerSimonian-Laird pooling across traits. Running them yourself is the way to
see which of the three a strange tau\* came from.

`annotData()`, `frqData()`, `annotCols()` and `sldscResults()` read
the corresponding parts of an `SldscData` back out.

### LD scores from an existing reference

`computeLdScores()` derives per-variant LD scores from an `LdEigen` or
`LdScore`, optionally stratified by annotation:

```{r compute-ld-scores}
scores <- computeLdScores(ldEigenExample)
head(round(as.vector(scores[, 1]), 3))
```

This is the same quantity `buildLdScore()` stores: each variant's sum, over
its block, of ldsc's unbiased r² rather than the raw sample r², which
overstates LD on a finite panel. From an `LdEigen` the raw sum comes out of
the eigendecomposition as `sum_i V[j,i]^2 d[i]^2`, and the correction applies
to that sum exactly, so the two agree — worth knowing when you have one
object and need the other's input.

## Bridging the two tracks

`h2EstimateToSldscTrait()` converts an `H2Estimate` into the same list shape
`readSldscTrait()` produces, so an in-package estimate can be meta-analysed
alongside polyfun runs:

```{r bridge, eval = hasPlinkMatrix}
names(h2EstimateToSldscTrait(strat))
```

## Per-gene cis heritability

Given a `QtlSumStats`, `estimateLocalH2()` estimates each trait's
heritability in its cis window: one estimate per (study, context, trait) row,
from the row's own statistics and LD reference. Every estimator it runs is a
setting of one model: within the window, the statistics' covariance is the
LD-weighted genetic covariance plus a noise term. An `H2EstimateParam` says
which statistic is fitted, by which criterion, how the noise and the LD
reference's own sampling noise enter, and how the uncertainty is reported.
No setting is named after a method; these reproduce the published ones, LAVA
(Werme 2022), HDL-L (Li 2025, the default), FastHer (Svishcheva 2025, with the
null space and a profiled scale) and GREML:

| Method | Statistic / criterion | Noise / reference | Reports |
|---|---|---|---|
| LAVA | eigen / moments | tied / overlap factor | h2, p |
| HDL-L | eigen / likelihood | free / eigenvalue term | h2, p, intercept |
| FastHer | eigen / likelihood | tied / none | h2, SE, scale |
| GREML (`QtlDataset`) | phenotype / REML | tied / none | h2, SE |

The genome-wide estimators' criteria also fit one window: the eigen
regression (LDER's model, to convergence), the variant GLS (gLDSC's) and the
variant regression (S-LDSC's, as MESC fits it per gene), each with a standard
error. `?H2EstimateParam` lists every field and the settings that do not
belong together.

```{r cis-h2, eval = hasPlinkMatrix}
data(qtlSumStatsExample)
cis <- estimateLocalH2(qtlSumStatsExample)
cis
cis[[1]]
h2EstimateParam(cis)
heritabilityIntercept(cis)
# LAVA's settings, which read how much of the study the reference holds.
lava <- H2EstimateParam(
    criterion = "moments",
    noise = "tied",
    crossNoise = "supplied",
    effects = "fixed",
    referenceNoise = "overlapFactor",
    truncation = H2TruncationParam(
        of = "eigenvalues",
        maxPerSample = 0.75,
        minimum = 2
    ),
    sampleSize = "mean",
    inference = "beta"
)
estimateLocalH2(qtlSumStatsExample, lava, referenceOverlap = 1)
```

Each row's element is the window its estimate covers: the row's `region`,
or with `cisWindow` the trait's position widened by that much on each side.
Every setting reads `z` as a t statistic and converts it exactly to the
correlation, since \(z / \sqrt{n}\) overstates a strong QTL's. The default,
HDL-L's likelihood, fits the statistics rotated onto the LD components that
cover 99% of the variant count, in the heritability and a free intercept.
Whether LD is the study's own is not a yes or no, and the intercept absorbs the
part of the reference's own noise that depends on how many of the study's
samples it holds, so the default needs no `referenceOverlap`. LAVA's moments
do: their noise term depends on how far the reference's LD lies from the
study's, and `referenceOverlap` is the share of the study's samples in the
reference. It defaults to 0, and with a reference of thousands it hardly
matters. Set it when the LD comes from the study's own samples or a small
cohort holding them, as here, where it is 1; at 0 such an estimate comes out
far too low, and a warning says so. Each estimate under the overlap factor
records the value it took in its `reference_overlap` column.
LAVA itself withholds its estimate where the components outnumber a tenth of
the sample size, which a cis window's usually do at QTL sample sizes;
`estimateLocalH2()` reports it at any size. The overlap factor and the
eigenvalue term read the reference's sample size, so an `LdMatrix` reference
must record `nSamples` for them. The likelihood with the null space, FastHer's,
assumes in-sample LD (HEELS maximizes the same one): where the reference's rank
or the statistics reach the study's sample size, as they can with LD from
outside the study, its estimate is `NA`, with a warning. Its standard error
assumes an infinitesimal architecture and is too small with few causal
variants.

### From individual-level data

Given a `QtlDataset`, `estimateLocalH2()` estimates each trait's heritability
on its own genotypes, over the window, samples, filters and residualized
genotypes and phenotype that `twasWeightsPipeline()` fits it on. The
summary-statistic settings read each variant's marginal statistic in-sample,
the genotypes being their own LD, so LAVA's estimate is the adjusted R^2 of
the trait on the genotypes' components. The phenotype statistic with REML is
GREML, the restricted maximum likelihood of the genetic and residual variances
on the window's relationship matrix (`qgg::greml`, with `GremlOptions()` for
its arguments), as FUSION estimates a gene's.

```{r cis-h2-individual, eval = hasPlinkMatrix}
data(qtlDatasetExample)
estimateLocalH2(qtlDatasetExample, cisWindow = 1e6)
```

```{r cis-h2-greml, eval = hasQgg && hasPlinkMatrix}
greml <- H2EstimateParam(
    statistic = "phenotype",
    criterion = "reml",
    noise = "tied",
    referenceNoise = "none",
    inference = "information"
)
estimateLocalH2(qtlDatasetExample, greml, cisWindow = 1e6)
```

### Starting other methods from it

The Bayesian alphabet's TWAS weights (`bayesA` to `bayesR`), LDpred2 and
SuSiE-RSS fine-mapping can start from a trait's heritability. The alphabet's
engines set their starting variances and the scales of their priors from a
guess of 0.5, which a cis window's heritability is usually far below, and
SuSiE-RSS holds its residual variance at 1 on z statistics, where the true one
is 1 minus the heritability. Give `twasWeightsPipeline()` or
`fineMappingPipeline()` either `h2EstimateParam`, settings to estimate each
trait's under first, on the variants and LD its methods fit, or
`h2Estimate`: one number for every trait, or the `H2Estimate` that
`estimateLocalH2()` returns, which gives each trait the value estimated
earlier. The weight functions take the same two (LDpred2-grid takes its own
grid as `h2Grid`).

```{r h2-first, eval=FALSE}
twasWeightsPipeline(
    qtlDatasetExample,
    methods = "bayesR",
    h2EstimateParam = greml
)
fineMappingPipeline(
    qtlSumStatsExample,
    methods = "susie",
    h2Estimate = estimateLocalH2(qtlSumStatsExample, referenceOverlap = 1)
)
```

## Local genetic correlation

`estimateLocalRg()` estimates the genetic covariance and correlation of
pairs of conditions in each cis window: each gene's contexts by default
(`jointSpecification` pairs along other axes), or each QTL condition with a
GWAS in its window (`gwas`). Each pair is fitted in two steps, each
condition's heritability and own noise as `estimateLocalH2()` fits them, then
the covariance with those held, under the same settings. The two
conditions' statistics also share noise through samples they share, which
`crossNoise` sets: fitted in the window (`"window"`, the default with HDL-L's
settings), supplied as `noiseCorrelation` (as `mashResidualCorrelation()`
returns one), tied on a `QtlDataset` to the phenotypes' correlation on the
donors both conditions have (`"tied"`), or none (`"zero"`). Per gene, local
rg at QTL sample sizes is rarely powered on its own; the summaries across
genes below are what it is mostly for.

```{r local-rg, eval = hasPlinkMatrix}
data(qtlSumStatsMulticontextExample)
rg <- estimateLocalRg(qtlSumStatsMulticontextExample)
rg
rg$noise_correlation
```

Under the likelihood, `H2LikelihoodParam(jointFit = TRUE)` fits a gene's
three or more contexts at once, so that their genetic correlation matrix is
one. With `conditional = TRUE` each pair is then given the gene's other
contexts, as LAVA's partial correlation and multiple regression read them:
rg is the partial genetic correlation, and `r2_1` and `r2_2` the share of
each context's genetic variance that the others explain.

```{r local-rg-joint, eval = hasPlinkMatrix}
joint <- H2EstimateParam(
    criterion = "likelihood",
    noise = "free",
    crossNoise = "window",
    referenceNoise = "eigenTerm",
    truncation = H2TruncationParam(
        of = "variants",
        maxPerSample = NULL,
        minimum = 1
    ),
    sampleSize = "median",
    inference = "lrt",
    procedures = H2LikelihoodParam(jointFit = TRUE)
)
given <- estimateLocalRg(
    qtlSumStatsMulticontextExample,
    param = joint,
    conditional = TRUE
)
S4Vectors::mcols(given)[
    c("context_1", "context_2", "rg", "p_value", "r2_1", "r2_2")
]
```

Conditions whose statistics sit on different LD references -- QTL studies
of different ancestries, each row of a `QtlSumStats` naming its own
reference, the studies of a `MultiStudyQtlDataset` on their own genotypes, or
a GWAS whose rows name its own panel -- are fitted each on its own
reference: their genetic term is R1 G12 R2 / M on the per-SD scale, and the
noise of whatever samples they share takes the average of the two LDs,
(R1 + R2) / 2, as its shape. How many samples two studies share is rarely
known, so every `crossNoise` applies as on one reference, and the default
fits it in the window; for studies of different populations it should come
out near none. Each setting has a two-reference form, and a group of three
or more is fitted at once on all its conditions' statistics. Studies of
different ancestries pair along the study axis:

```{r local-rg-ancestry, eval = FALSE}
estimateLocalRg(studies, jointSpecification = "study")
```

The estimate is of the correlation of per-SD effects, on the variants both
references carry; per gene at QTL sample sizes it is imprecise, and its use
is mostly across genes.

Two fields of `H2EstimateParam()` say how the effects are read. `alpha`, the
frequency exponent, weighs each variant's effect variance by its
heterozygosity in the reference, [2p(1 - p)]^(1 + alpha): the default -1
weighs every variant alike (per-SD effects), 0 is the per-allele model, and
LDAK's -0.25 lies between. Across ancestries, `alpha = 0` estimates the
correlation of per-allele effects; the reference must record its allele
frequencies (an `LdMatrix`'s `AF`, a genotype panel, or a dataset's own
genotypes). `effects` sets how the moments read a window: `"random"` (the
default) draws the window's genetic components, as the likelihood and the
regressions model them, and `"fixed"` is LAVA's reading, the components held
fixed, as LAVA's settings take it.

Across genes, `summarizeLocalRg()` gives each pair of contexts one
correlation: the ratio of the summed covariances to the root of the product
of the summed heritabilities (`"pooled"`, with a jackknife over genes), the
mean of the genes' rg over those whose heritabilities exceed `minH2`
(`"mean"`), and one rg for every gene from their summed likelihoods
(`"shared"`, under the likelihood). The pooled ratio needs each gene's
estimates unbounded, as the moments' and the regressions' are; the
likelihood's bounds pull it low. Given a fitted mash model (`mashModel`), it
reports mash's prior correlation of the two contexts beside them. The
example holds one gene, so each summary is that gene's.

```{r local-rg-summary, eval = hasPlinkMatrix}
summarizeLocalRg(rg)
```
